description: Software engineering student at the University of Lahore. I work in Python, data pipelines and time-series analysis. For this challenge we'll build a web tool that pulls NASA Earth data (MERRA-2, GPM, MODIS) for a region, plots it over time, and tests whether the trend is significant (Mann-Kendall). Looking for teammates who know data visualization, front-end work, or Earth science. Joining virtually.
summary: TrendScope is a global atlas of tested trends in NASA Earth data. For any place on the planet it answers the four questions in the challenge: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant. We turned 19 NASA variables into yearly series for every 1° grid cell, most of them from 1981 to 2025. They range from air and wet-bulb temperature to rainfall, soil water, sea ice, ozone, aerosols, groundwater from GRACE and vegetation from MODIS. Each cell gets a Sen slope and a Mann-Kendall test corrected for year-to-year memory. Testing 50,000 places at once produces false alarms by chance, so every map is filtered with false discovery rate control, and places where the change could be chance are hatched. A user can click a place, type a question, or follow a guided case file, and gets a verdict they can read and cite. In Lahore, our home region, humid heat is rising 0.57 °C per decade with very strong evidence. NASA's reanalysis and its weather-station record disagree about plain air temperature there, and the app shows both. GRACE shows parts of Punjab losing up to 40 cm of stored water per decade.
details:
What it does

The atlas is a 3D globe that shows the trend of any of the 19 variables, from 1981 to 2025 for most of them and from 2001 or 2003 for the newer satellite records. Trends that pass the false discovery test are drawn in solid colour, and change that could be chance is hatched. A year-by-year mode plays each year's difference from the 1981 to 2010 average.

Clicking a place opens an investigation that runs in the browser. It reports the Sen slope per decade with its 95% interval, a Mann-Kendall test with a conservative Yue and Wang correction for autocorrelation, Kendall's tau, a least-squares check and a Pettitt change point. It also gives the Weatherhead detection time, the number of years of record a trend of this size needs before it can be detected, so a "no trend yet" result still tells you something. Time-window buttons re-run every test on part of the record, which shows, for example, Antarctic ozone falling sharply until 2000 and then holding steady. Live monthly data from NASA POWER at that exact point adds a seasonal fingerprint. An independent NASA record gives a second opinion: GISTEMP weather stations against the MERRA-2 temperature, or GPCP satellites and rain gauges against MERRA-2 rainfall. A scan ranks every other variable at the same place by the strength of its evidence.

Detective mode asks two questions, what to investigate and where, and accepts either a named place or a kind of place such as a megacity, farmland or desert. It returns a ranked report of what is changing there and the variables scientists usually watch in that landscape.

The search box also takes questions such as "Is Karachi getting more humid?". A small language model reads only the place and the variable. Every number comes from the NASA data and the tests.

The opposite-fates view links the strongest significant rise and the strongest significant fall of a variable anywhere on Earth. The challenge brief points out that one process can push two regions in opposite directions, and this view shows it directly.

Six case files walk through real investigations that draw on peer-reviewed research and are computed live from the data: humid heat and groundwater in Lahore, Arctic amplification, the ozone hole and why the time window matters, opposite rainfall trends in the Sahel and south-west Australia, dimming and brightening of sunlight, and Chile's megadrought.

The method page explains every test twice, once in plain language and once with formulas. Its shuffle test scrambles Lahore's real data 600 times so a student can see what a p-value measures.

How it works

A Python pipeline reads NASA POWER's analysis-ready Zarr archive on AWS Open Data (MERRA-2 and CERES SYN1deg), NASA GISS GISTEMP v4, GPCP v2.3, GRACE/GRACE-FO mascons and MODIS MOD13C2 through NASA Earthdata. It builds annual values for every grid cell and runs the trend tests on all cells at once with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control at q = 0.10 (Wilks 2016). The web app (React, TypeScript, a custom three.js WebGL globe, d3) repeats the same tests in TypeScript, so the map and the verdict for a clicked place always agree. The TypeScript statistics are checked against pymannkendall reference values in 487 automated tests. The app is hosted for free on Cloudflare Pages with no server that has to wake up, and the processed maps ship with it, so it keeps working when a NASA service is slow.

Why it matters

Heat action plans, water allocation and crop planning all depend on knowing whether a change is real. Today that answer usually takes a scientist who can code and knows which data portal to use. TrendScope gives a student or a city planner a tested answer in seconds. Along the way it teaches the checks that make an answer trustworthy: removing the seasons, allowing for year-to-year memory, correcting for testing many places at once, and comparing with a second, independent record.

Tools and languages

Python (NumPy, xarray, pymannkendall for validation), TypeScript, React, three.js, d3, Vite, Cloudflare Pages and Workers AI, GitHub Actions. The code is open under the MIT licence: https://github.com/abuhuraira99/trendscope-nasa-space-apps-2026
